prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network scored 0 and always chooses DONE at step 1, so it learned nothing. Two likely causes. (1) Mirror mismatch: a brick chosen at column x lands at column X-dx-x. The per-cell scores are aligned with the chosen anchor, so a local convolution cannot connect an anchor to the features at its landing cells. With the network unable to tell good placements from bad, it settles on DONE. (2) Pull toward DONE: random placements earn negative reward, while DONE earns 0 and gets a large positive advantage, so the policy can lock onto DONE before it learns useful placements. Mirroring the trunk's features left-to-right after the learned trunk lines column x up exactly with the cells it fills, including the 2-wide footprints, so the existing footprint pooling works unchanged. This round tests the mirrored features with and without a recipe meant to resist the DONE collapse, plus a learned column remapping as a more general alternative.

### Round 2
The mirror rule was the main blocker. Without a fixed left-right flip, both runs collapsed to DONE at step 1: the starting network and the learned column mixer (r1c3) each scored 0.000. Concatenating a flipped copy of the trunk features lines up each anchor's score with the cells where the brick actually lands. That gave 0.53 (r1c1). Adding ppo_epochs 2 and ent_coef 0.02 raised it to 0.84 (r1c2). Both r1c2 seeds were high (0.87 and 0.80), and the gain is well beyond noise. In r1c2, IoU is 0.98 but exact success is 0.84, so most failures are a few wrong cells. Its training success was still rising at the end (0.64 → 0.78), so the run looks short of samples. This round makes three single changes to r1c2: (1) ppo_epochs 1, giving about 1.9x more samples; (2) a deeper trunk with a wider receptive field; (3) a longer horizon (gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95) so the +1 exact-build bonus has more pull on early choices.

### Round 3
The mirror rule was the main obstacle. Once the head could see the flipped features (flip-concat), success went from 0 to 0.53. After that, more samples mattered most. ppo_epochs 2 with ent_coef 0.02 reached 0.84, and ppo_epochs 1 reached 0.92 (seeds 0.93 and 0.91, so the result is consistent). A deeper trunk with 2 epochs scored 0.72, because extra compute cost samples. A longer horizon (gamma 0.99) was unstable, with seeds at 0.16 and 0.79. A learned column mixer collapsed to DONE.

Flipping the whole trunk is exact and cheaper. A brick dx wide at anchor x lands on columns 8-dx-x .. 7-x. In mirrored coordinates those are columns x .. x+dx-1, which matches the head's pooling window. So flipping right after the 1x1 learned stem gives r = 1.0 and about 426k steps, up from 397k. Training success levelled off at about 0.85 over the last quarter. The other two trials test more gradient steps per sample and more trunk capacity under the 1-epoch recipe.

### Round 4
The left-right mirror rule is the main obstacle. A fixed flip (in the head, or right after the stem) unlocks learning. A learned column mixer collapsed to DONE. After that, the recipe matters most: going from 2 PPO epochs to 1 means more fresh samples (0.84 to 0.92), and 64 minibatches give more gradient steps per sample (0.897 to 0.949 for the flip-after-stem net). Extra depth hurts: it costs samples, and one deeper seed collapsed to 0.08. gamma 0.99 was unstable. At the best trial's end, training success was still rising (0.91), so the remaining gains probably come from better use of samples or cheap context, not bigger trunks. Seed spread at the top is about ±0.01–0.02, so gains under about 0.02 are not reliable. For this final round I make one change each to the best trial r3c2: a higher learning rate, broadcast global context into the placement head, and a dilated second convolution for a wider view at the same compute.

## Trial it ended with
name: flip after stem, 64 minibatches
hypothesis: Same network as the flip-after-stem candidate, but with n_minibatches 64 instead of 32. With one epoch, this doubles the gradient steps per sample (64-sample minibatches). Training success levelled off at about 0.85 while the learning rate decayed, so more optimiser steps on the same fresh data should extract more from each sample. Refuted if this is not clearly above the plain flip-after-stem candidate, or if one seed becomes unstable.
